articles.title: R2Socks
articles.author: Kitploit
articles.content:
SOCKS5 proxy tunneled through Cloudflare R2 object storage, with Python and dependency-free C++ agents relaying TCP traffic via encrypted R2 objects for covert access.
SOCKS5 proxy tunneled through Cloudflare R2 buckets.
[Client App] ◄─SOCKS5─► [Proxy] ◄─── R2 Bucket ───► [Agent] ◄─TCP─► [Target]
The proxy runs a local SOCKS5 server on the operator's machine. Every CONNECT request is serialized as binary packets and stored as R2 objects. The agent polls the same bucket from the target network, picks up connection requests, establishes real TCP connections, and relays data back through R2.
| Component | Language | File | Description | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Proxy | Python | r2socks.py | SOCKS5 server (operator side) | 
| Agent | Python | r2socks.py | Target-side relay (agent mode) | 
| Agent | C++ | r2agent.cpp | Standalone Windows agent, zero dependencies | 
The C++ agent is protocol-compatible with the Python proxy. It uses only Windows-native APIs (WinHTTP, bcrypt, Winsock2) no external libraries required.
dash.cloudflare.com/<ACCOUNT_ID>/r2/...pip install boto3
python r2socks.py proxy -b my-bucket -a <account_id> \
    --access-key <R2_ACCESS_KEY> --secret-key <R2_SECRET_KEY>
The proxy generates a channel ID and prints the command to start the agent.
Python agent:
python r2socks.py agent -b my-bucket -a <account_id> -c <channel_id> \
    --access-key <R2_ACCESS_KEY> --secret-key <R2_SECRET_KEY>
C++ agent (Windows):
.\r2agent.exe -b my-bucket -a <account_id> -c <channel_id> -k <access_key> -s <secret_key>
python r2socks.py proxy [options]
Required:
  -b, --bucket BUCKET         R2 bucket name
  -a, --account-id ID         Cloudflare account ID
Optional:
  -c, --channel ID            Channel ID (auto-generated if omitted)
  -l, --listen ADDR           Listen address (default: 127.0.0.1:1080)
  --access-key KEY            R2 API token Access Key ID
  --secret-key KEY            R2 API token Secret Access Key
  --socks-user USER           Enable SOCKS5 user/pass authentication
  --socks-pass PASS           SOCKS5 password
  -p, --password PWD          AES-256-GCM encryption password
  -v, --verbose               Debug logging
Python:
python r2socks.py agent [options]
Required:
  -b, --bucket BUCKET         R2 bucket name
  -a, --account-id ID         Cloudflare account ID
  -c, --channel ID            Channel ID (from proxy output)
C++ (Windows):
r2agent.exe [options]
Required:
  -b, --bucket BUCKET         R2 bucket name
  -a, --account-id ID         Cloudflare account ID
  -c, --channel ID            Channel ID (from proxy output)
Credentials (flags override env vars):
  -k, --access-key KEY        R2 API token Access Key ID
  -s, --secret-key KEY        R2 API token Secret Access Key
Optional:
  -v, --verbose               Debug logging
Remove all R2 objects from a channel when done:
python r2socks.py clean -b my-bucket -a <account_id> -c <channel_id>
Binary packet format shared between proxy and agent:
┌──────────┬────────────────────┬────────────┬──────────────────┐
│ CMD (1B) │ ConnectionID (16B) │ Len (4B BE)│ Payload (var)    │
└──────────┴────────────────────┴────────────┴──────────────────┘
Multiple packets are batched into a single R2 object (up to 4MB) to reduce API calls. Objects are named with microsecond timestamps for ordering and deleted after consumption.
Optional AES-256-GCM encryption for all R2 payloads:
pip install cryptography
# Both sides must use the same password
python r2socks.py proxy -b bucket -a account_id -p "my-secret-password"
python r2socks.py agent -b bucket -a account_id -c channel -p "my-secret-password"
The key is derived using PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations.
From a Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt:
cl /std:c++17 /EHsc /O2 r2agent.cpp /link ws2_32.lib winhttp.lib bcrypt.lib
Both proxy and agent use adaptive sleep intervals:
This balances responsiveness against API call volume. Stats are logged every 30 seconds showing active connections, objects transferred, and bytes moved.
SignatureDoesNotMatchw32tm /resync /force (Windows) or sudo ntpdate pool.ntp.org (Linux)RequestTimeTooSkewedAccessDenied
Proxy (Python):
boto3 (required)cryptography (optional, for encryption)
Agent (C++):
| Command | Code | Direction | Payload | 
|---|---|---|---|
| NEW | 0x01 | Proxy→Agent | ATYP + Address + Port | 
| ACK | 0x02 | Agent→Proxy | 1 byte status (0=success) | 
| DATA | 0x03 | Bidirectional | Raw TCP data (up to 1MB) | 
| CLOSE | 0x04 | Bidirectional | Empty | 
| PING | 0x05 | Bidirectional | Empty |
articles.summary:
A new SOCKS5 proxy tool leverages Cloudflare R2 object storage to tunnel TCP traffic, enabling covert network communication through encrypted binary packets stored as temporary bucket objects.

### Key Points
- The tool uses Python for the proxy and offers both Python and dependency-free C++ agents for Windows-based target systems.
- Communication relies on polling R2 buckets, where connection requests and data are serialized into binary packets and stored as objects.
- It supports optional AES-256-GCM encryption for payloads, utilizing PBKDF2-SHA256 key derivation with 600,000 iterations.
- The system employs adaptive sleep intervals and batching to balance network responsiveness with API call volume and efficiency.
- The C++ agent is built using native Windows APIs, including WinHTTP, bcrypt, and Winsock2, requiring no external library dependencies.

### Why it Matters
This technique demonstrates how cloud storage services can be repurposed as covert command-and-control channels to bypass traditional network security perimeters. Security teams should monitor for unusual traffic patterns or high-frequency object creation within R2 buckets that may indicate unauthorized data exfiltration or proxy activity.

articles.title: We asked our Gen Z and millennial reporters and editors about AI agents. Here's where they split.
articles.author: Martina Nacach Cowan Ros
articles.content:
Everyone is talking about AI agents — and Business Insider's reporters and editors are no different.
Agents go a step beyond chatbots and are capable of planning and achieving multi-step tasks. This can range from making a restaurant reservation to inviting a friend for lunch to buying clothes you are on the lookout for.
To get a sense of how members of different generations feel about the emerging world of AI agents, I, a Gen Z fellow on the Business Insider Economy team, talked to my colleagues, spanning from Gen Z to elder millennials, about their stances on the divisive topic.
While the younger generation expressed a lot of worries around privacy, the millennials in the group were cautiously optimistic about how agents could be helpful at work and at home.
The Gen Z consensus: Skepticism and privacy concerns
Many of my Gen Z peers agreed that growing up with technology made them more aware of its limitations and dangers — making them more hesitant about handing over their information to AI agents. They also seemed most concerned about privacy and scams.
The younger members of the Economy team aren't alone — a recent poll from the Pew Research Center found that Americans under age 30 are increasingly skeptical of AI's benefits.
Ayelet Sheffey, our Gen Z senior education reporter, said she was not open to handing over the control to an AI agent to get things she needed done.
"I'm hearing about people using AI and they're like feeding their bank information or personal things into a software — that just immediately turns me off," she said. "Not only for the privacy reasons, but also, I just don't trust anyone or anything else to get tasks done."
Allie Kelly, a Gen Z economy reporter, said that while being a reporter is a public-facing job, there is other information she prefers to keep private. While she is open to using it for professional purposes, she is more hesitant to use it for personal reasons, not knowing how the information she provides to the agent can be used.
"If I want an agent to analyze something, I will give it something specific to analyze — I'm not going to give it access to my inbox," she said. "It's not just my information; sometimes it's sources' information, so I just want to be cognizant of that."
Juliana Kaplan, a Gen Z senior reporter, said she is wary of handing her personal information over to companies that could have different incentives influencing how their AI agents work. She posed a rhetorical question: If a company with an AI agent had a deal with a credit card company, and she was using an agent to choose her next credit card, would it be influenced to recommend that one?
"I would have to do a lot of research into the amount of due diligence they have done with my information," she said. "At that point, I'm like, I can just do it myself."
Noah Sheidlower, a Gen Z senior economy reporter, said, "I'm all for efficiency and maximizing time I could be spending on things that are meaningful to me, but I don't fully trust giving up my authority and agency to make decisions. I've read stories of agents invading privacy and doing tasks it should not be doing that have harmful repercussions, and I want to stay in control as much as I can until the agents are more advanced."
Madison Hoff, a Gen Z economy reporter, said that while she sees the value of agents in helping manage work, she enjoys working on things herself. When looking for craft ideas in her free time, she said she enjoys the process of looking around her and finding ideas — even if an AI agent would help her do it more quickly.
"I rather just use the brain power a little more and do the research," she said.
Several of the Gen Z reporters said that while friends in creative fields were more hesitant to adopt AI agents, peers in finance, consulting, and tech-adjacent fields seemed more open to adopting them earlier.
The millennial consensus: Cautious optimism
The idea that AI agents still have a long way to go before they are accurate and efficient enough was shared by the Economy team's millennial editors, who held a more cautious optimism about the future of adopting agents to streamline workflows and team operations.
Bartie Scott, a millennial and economy deputy editor, said that while she has environmental concerns about using AI, she does see potential in using it to reduce her screen time — especially with voice agents.
"As someone who has a job that's on a screen, it can feel insurmountable sometimes," she said. "We have so much to do in modern life that you feel burned out — And I think this, maybe in an ideal world, could be like a solution to that."
Scott said that while she is not an early adopter of technology, once she has seen people she respects say the technology is trustworthy and easy to use, she might be inclined to dabble in it. Examples she thought of would be if she could get an agent to help brief her on her workday priorities and daily check-ins.
"If I could do all that with voice commands, that would kind of be a dream," she said.
Andy Kiersz, a millennial and senior economic data editor, agreed that he might be more in the mid-adopter camp than the early-adopter camp. If a "sufficiently long period of time" passes with no major data breaches and a situation like planning a trip arises where it would be useful, he said he would consider using an agent.
Kiersz sees some potential for agentic AI at work. "I could totally see putting an agent to go crawl repositories of economics papers and read through the abstracts," he said. He sees himself sending agents to do the "tedious side of the job," so he can focus on the "interesting side of the job."
Two millennials on the team had the most hands-on experience with these new toys.
Ryan Kailath, an elder millennial and senior editor, is a "big pointsmaxxer," as a member of many airline loyalty programs. Yet, finding awards when booking is always a hefty logistical task. So Kailath used Muse, the personal AI agent launched by Meta in early September, to see what all the fuss was about and look into booking for an upcoming trip.
Although the AI agent took the lead, it encountered many problems that Kailath had to resolve manually, such as login credentials and two-factor authentication codes required to continue the search.
"My one test case where I thought, 'Here's a big friction in my life, maybe an agent could make this friction easier,' it failed miserably," he said. Yet, Kailath said that if it improved in the future, he would no doubt use it.
Our Senior Reporter, Jacob Zinkula, also had a brief 10-minute encounter with Muse. Zinkula, a young millennial, downloaded the app to see if it could help him get a future reservation at a high-demand restaurant for the Christmas season, but has yet to figure it out. Caught in the cusp of the Gen Z and millennial generations, he is more cautious about letting an AI agent make financial decisions on its own, but is open to waiting to see how they could develop and be useful in the future.
"I try to be open but skeptical," he said. "It doesn't feel like there's an immediate need for me to like jump onto it too soon. That said, I'm open to ways it could be helpful going forward. For better or worse, this stuff's probably not going away."
articles.summary:
Business Insider reporters from Gen Z and millennial generations express differing levels of skepticism and optimism regarding the adoption of AI agents for personal and professional tasks.

### Key Points
- AI agents are designed to perform multi-step tasks like booking travel or managing schedules, moving beyond the capabilities of standard chatbots.
- Gen Z staff cited significant concerns regarding data privacy, potential scams, and the loss of personal agency when delegating tasks to automated software.
- Millennial editors expressed cautious optimism, viewing AI agents as potential tools to reduce screen time and automate tedious professional workflows.
- Practical testing of Meta’s Muse AI agent revealed current limitations, including failures with two-factor authentication and complex logistical tasks.
- Pew Research Center data indicates that Americans under age 30 are increasingly skeptical of the overall benefits provided by artificial intelligence.

### Why it Matters
The divide between generational attitudes highlights the significant trust barriers that developers must overcome to achieve widespread consumer adoption of agentic AI. As these tools evolve, their ability to balance efficiency with data security will determine whether they become essential productivity assistants or remain niche technologies.

articles.title: The AI safety debate is confusing. Here's our guide to the different factions
articles.author: Katie McQue
articles.content:
The AI safety debate is confusing. Here's our guide to the different factions
The debate over the potential benefits and safety risks of accelerating artificial intelligence development reached a crescendo this month, as supporters and critics of the technology clashed over warnings that increasingly powerful AI could pose existential risks to humanity.
On September 8, Jacob Coxon, a researcher-turned-whistleblower, publicly resigned from major AI firm Anthropic after a previous stint at OpenAI, accusing the companies of "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
Coxon's claims supercharged an ongoing debate over the potential damage AI could wreak on society and prompted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and other AI CEOs to call for a slowdown in AI development.
Over the past two months, companies including OpenAI and Anthropic disclosed multiple incidents in which their AI agents accessed the internet when they weren't supposed to and carried out unapproved activities. In OpenAI's case, swarms of agents worked together to hack the open-source software platform Hugging Face and OpenAI itself, without alerting humans.
The debate over the safety of AI and whether and how it should be regulated is not a simple clash between two opposing sides. There are multiple factions with a variety of goals and assessments about the technology's promise, dangers and how it should be governed. Here are the main arguments shaping that debate.
Effective accelerationists and the tech right
Those who have an aggressively optimistic worldview of AI are often referred to as effective accelerationists (sometimes shortened to e/acc) – a term reflecting their belief that AI should be rapidly advanced.
People belonging to the faction are emphatically optimistic about AI and its future benefits to society. They believe that the technology can propel medical advancements, boost economic productivity, increase living standards, and automate dangerous or undesirable work. To achieve this, they argue that AI development should be accelerated, not restricted.
Effective accelerationists' ideology overlaps with that of the "tech right", in that both camps wholeheartedly believe in accelerating AI development and deployment and minimize critics' concerns over safety and security.
However, the tech right takes a more nationalistic stance, championing U.S. dominance in the global AI race. Like effective accelerationists, they believe that AI research and deployment should be unencumbered by regulation, arguing that could slow innovation or allow adversarial governments such as China to overtake the U.S. in the AI race.
The tech right's philosophy is represented by figures such as former White House AI and cryptocurrency advisor David Sacks, whose views remain influential with the Trump administration. Other significant players include venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman. The three founded the Leading the Future super PAC to support pro-AI political candidates, and campaign against those who advocate for regulation.
Andreessen also penned a 2023 widely-read blog post titled "Why AI Will Save the World," in which he claimed that fears of AI triggering mass unemployment are overstated. He argued that previous waves of automation ultimately created more jobs and economic activity than they eliminated, and the fears of existential risk are overblown.
Recently, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, whose chips are used by most AI companies, has emerged as one of the industry's leading voices pushing back against calls for a slowdown and urging a light regulatory approach.
Populist right
AI has exposed an ideological split within President Trump's political coalition. While Trump and his advisers overwhelmingly favor accelerating AI, parts of his MAGA base believe the powerful corporations he has aligned himself with could undermine the U.S. economy.
Figures including former Trump strategist Steve Bannon and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson have been vocal about potential job losses, the tech industry's political power, child safety and threats to traditional social and religious values.
This month, Bannon formed an unlikely partnership with independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, a socialist, to call for significant restrictions on AI development, government oversight and corporate accountability at the Pro-Human Assembly conference in Washington, D.C.
Still, the two have differing stances on what any of those measures should look like. Sanders called for an immediate pause on AI development until clear safety rules are established by scientists, a permanent ban on the development of artificial "superintelligence" (AI systems that are more intelligent than humans in all domains), and an international treaty with China in an effort to avoid an AI arms race. Bannon, meanwhile, argued for slowing the pace of AI development, the formation of a national regulatory organization and for cutting off China from U.S. AI technology.
"So why are we letting the Chinese Communist Party drive us? Oh, we have to do this or China wins," said Bannon in his speech at the event in Washington. "We should quarantine now every aspect of the ecosystem of artificial intelligence away from the Chinese Communist Party today. We should cut them off."
Safetyists
Safetyists are primarily concerned with the potential risks of the rapid advancement of AI. Their worries center on the possibility of catastrophic or existential outcomes, such as the death of humanity at the hands of autonomous machines.
High-profile members of the safetyist community include Geoffrey Hinton, who is commonly referred to as the "Godfather of AI" because of his pioneering work in deep learning that helped launch the modern era of AI. In recent years, Hinton, who previously worked at Google, has issued a series of warnings about existential risks associated with AI, particularly if an AI model surpasses human intelligence and becomes autonomous.
Another vocal AI safetyist is Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI and co-author of AI 2027, a paper published last year that discusses how super-intelligent AI could lead to human extinction by the mid-2030s.
Effective altruists
Effective altruists (often shortened to "EA") generally believe in maximizing humanity's long-term welfare. The movement originally focused on material ways to reduce global poverty. But more recently, many EA thinkers have focused their concerns on the possibility of existential risks from advanced AI and other potential societal-scale disasters such as nuclear war, climate change and pandemics. They particularly worry about the consequences for future generations. People from the EA camp prioritize AI safety, alignment – which is the science of making sure AI systems behave in a way that is reflective of human values and in line with safety rules – and reducing the probability of catastrophic outcomes.
The key difference between EAs and safetyists is that EAs generally provide funding for AI safety research and risk mitigation, whereas safetyists are researchers and advocates undertaking AI safety work and publicly calling for regulation.
Other AI factions often derisively describe effective altruists as so-called "AI Doomers." EA has also become a focus of criticism from the Trump administration since Coxon's resignation from Anthropic.
"Americanism, not effective altruism. The United States will continue to be AI DOMINANT!" said one Defense Department post this month.
Well-known people in the EA movement include Eliezer Yudkowsky, co-founder of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), which focuses on mathematical approaches to making advanced AI systems safe. He is also the author of Harry Potter fan fiction that helped popularize ideas associated with EA. Holden Karnofsky, an American entrepreneur and philanthropist, founded Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), an organization that funds causes central to the EA mission, including AI and biosecurity. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is considered to be aligned with effective altruism. Karnofsky also works at Anthropic and is married to Daniela Amodei, who is a co-founder of Anthropic and the sister of Dario Amodei, the CEO.
Another high-profile supporter of the EA movement is Sam Bankman-Fried, who founded major cryptocurrency exchange FTX. In 2023, he was convicted of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy related to the misuse of customer and investor funds and is currently serving a 25-year prison sentence.
AI ethics
The AI ethics camp argues that society should focus on the harms AI is already causing, rather than on hypothetical existential risks. Some proponents contend that emphasizing existential threats from a hypothetical future superintelligence can serve as a distraction from the more immediate harms and accountability issues surrounding AI today.
AI ethicists' concerns include how AI systems can be biased due to the content of their training data, for example, the ways in which AI facial recognition or job application systems might perpetuate existing societal biases. They are also concerned with how AI could be used to exploit workers and to enable mass surveillance, as well as about the environmental costs of data centers, autonomous weapons, and the concentration of power among technology companies.
A notable voice of the AI ethics faction is Timnit Gebru, a computer scientist and former co-lead of Google's Ethical AI team. Gebru left the company in 2020 because of a dispute with the company over a research paper she wrote exposing problems with large language models (LLMs), including their tendency to generate harmful or misleading language.
AI as a normal technology
People belonging to the "AI as a Normal Technology" group reject both the utopian and dystopian narratives about AI. Instead, this faction sees AI as a powerful but ultimately normal technology, comparable to the internet or electricity. They believe the focus should be on understanding and regulating specific applications and harms instead of treating AI as an unprecedented threat or as a path to inevitable superintelligence.
Notable people associated with this worldview include Fei-Fei Li, a computer scientist and co-director of the Stanford Human-Centered AI Institute. Li is famous for creating ImageNet, a vastly large dataset of images which provided the training data for large neural networks, which led to several major developments in AI.
Katie McQue's reporting is supported by the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism, which is a grantee of Coefficient Giving. Neither Tarbell nor Coefficient have any editorial input into her work.
articles.summary:
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has triggered a complex global debate, dividing experts and policymakers into distinct factions regarding the technology's existential risks and potential societal benefits.

### Key Points
- Whistleblower Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing concerns that companies are recklessly racing toward self-improving superintelligence.
- "Effective accelerationists" and the "tech right" advocate for rapid development to ensure U.S. dominance and economic growth, opposing restrictive regulations.
- "Safetyists" and "effective altruists" prioritize long-term risk mitigation, fearing that autonomous AI systems could eventually pose existential threats to humanity.
- The "AI ethics" faction argues that current industry focus on hypothetical future risks distracts from immediate harms like algorithmic bias, surveillance, and labor exploitation.
- An "AI as a normal technology" group, including Stanford’s Fei-Fei Li, views AI as a tool comparable to electricity, favoring application-specific regulation over existential alarmism.
- Political figures like Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon have formed an unlikely coalition to demand government oversight and corporate accountability for AI development.

### Why it Matters
The fragmentation of the AI safety debate complicates efforts to establish a unified regulatory framework, leaving policymakers caught between competing visions of innovation and risk. This ideological divide directly influences corporate strategy, government funding priorities, and the future of international AI governance.

articles.title: Enshittification Has a New Mascot, and He’s Teaming Up With Death in a Hilarious Ad Campaign
articles.author: Joe Hindy
articles.content:
Imagine, if you will, a pale figure of Death, dressed in a black robe holding a scythe, alongside a handsome, lumberjack-looking Nordic fella who goes by the name Enshittificator. As partners in crime, they conspire to make your life suck, all because they have the power to make digital products and services worse.
If that piques your interest — and maybe sounds too much like real life — a new “anti-enshittification” ad campaign is worth a few minutes of your time.
The term “enshittification” was popularized in 2022 by author and activist Cory Doctorow, and its massive cultural surge earned it a place in Merriam-Webster’s slang hub last year. Enshittification is a deliberate process, designed by companies to maximize profit.
More from CNET
It starts with luring you to a product or service, then making it so good that you become completely dependent on it. The next step is to pull the rug out from under you by hiding basic features behind a paywall, reducing overall quality and squeezing you for every last dime while providing as little value as possible.
The Death and Enshittificator video above, released on YouTube in mid-September, is the second of a series from the Norwegian Consumer Council, an independent, government-funded nonprofit that advocates for consumer rights. The main character, the Enshittificator, is a bearded Nordic man who says in the first video, released in February, that his “job is to make things shitty.”
The initial video concludes with Mr. Enshittificator getting into a car accident because he didn’t pay a subscription for his braking system, a scenario he appeared to find amusing. In the second video, he meets Death in the hospital, and the two enter into a business relationship. (He now dons a yellow hazmat suit to stay alive.)
The duo spends time making every conceivable product worse, from TVs and toothbrushes to smartphone storage. They point out that products with long lifespans, like the famously indestructible Nokia 3310 — which makes a cameo appearance — only generate revenue once. If companies want a profitable business model, however, they have to use low-quality materials, ensure products can’t be fixed and stop issuing updates.
“Look at all the companies that used to make solid products,” the Enshittificator said. “Where are they now?”
“Dead,” Death said, and they share a knowing smile.
The Norwegian Consumer Council’s ads are part of its Breaking Free initiative, a multipronged policy approach to make technology work in favor of consumers, rather than against them. The campaign craftily relies on dark humor to detail how enshittification affects everyday life, from paid subscription models to planned obsolescence, which forces you to buy newer devices.
The videos are also a strikingly accurate commentary on the dismal state of products and gadgets in the digital age. Prices go up while reliability plummets. Companies rely on shady advertising tactics and dodge consumer protection rights.
Doctorow himself collaborated with the nonprofit to help launch the series, which he’s immensely pleased with. In an email to CNET, he said, “The idea that firms’ market power means that they can worsen their offerings with impunity, combined with the minor license to vulgarity of my dirty little word, have proven a winning combination for helping people direct their anger in the right direction.”
Real life (and death)
The enshittification process is relatable and real. In 2020, Apple agreed to pay up to $500 million to settle the landmark “batterygate” class action lawsuit over allegations that it secretly slowed down older iPhone models through software updates. Powerful tech companies have poured massive amounts of money into lobbying against right-to-repair laws, preventing customers from fixing their own devices when they break.
“It’s really important that the products can’t be fixed,” said the Enshittificator. “It breaks, then it dies, so you have to buy a new one. And another one. And another one. And another one. And another one.”
“This way, we’re actually slowly killing the planet as well,” a smiling Death said, helpfully chiming in.
The videos also satirize how digital services slowly degrade over time. In one scene, the Enshittificator tells an employee, “The 1,000 pictures of your deceased mother are mine, and you’re going to pay for them.” It’s a direct nod to Google Photos’ 2021 policy shift, which ended free unlimited storage and capped free accounts at 15GB, requiring users to get a subscription to keep already uploaded photos on the platform.
Another scene takes a jab at automakers who sell you basic functionality as an add-on subscription service.
“I don’t have any more money. You have me in the palm of your hand,” said the Enshittificator in a fake presentation about selling cars. “You can crush me. So what do you do? Updates. Radio? Premium feature. Heating? Premium feature. Now I have a shitty car, and I can’t afford a new one, but what I can afford is a small monthly payment!”
This is a reference to BMW’s controversial microtransaction model, where it tried to make heated seats and other in-car features part of a subscription plan. While intense consumer backlash forced the German automaker to walk back some of the “add-ons,” several features remain behind a paywall. Other brands have followed suit — Hyundai’s BlueLink and Kia Connect require paid plans to use remote start. For a period, both manufacturers even omitted the remote-start button from the physical key fob, completely blocking owners from using the feature for free.
Can it be fixed?
It’s important, though a little depressing, to imagine how much better life would be if companies actually invested money into making their products better, safer and longer-lasting — and not just more profitable for them.
In its Breaking Free: Pathways to a Fair Technological Future report, the Norwegian Consumer Council argues that major tech business models “are often fundamentally incompatible with consumer and human rights.” To dismantle the “walled gardens run by Big Tech feudalists” and end dependence on Big Tech, the nonprofit is pushing for policy reforms built around a three-pronged strategy based on democratic values and principles of openness.
The first is interoperability, which would force platforms to interface with one another. This is already taking shape under the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required Apple to allow third-party app stores and mandated Meta to support external chats in WhatsApp,
Next comes portability, which would allow users to move their contacts, content, photos and anything else to rival services. A subscriber fed up with Spotify adding AI features, for instance, would be able to switch to YouTube Music or Apple Music without losing their saved playlists, thereby eliminating platform lock-in.
Finally, and arguably the most difficult to implement, is decentralization of social media, which could shift social media away from single-entity corporate control toward open networks like the Fediverse (which powers platforms such as Mastodon). Though still evolving as protocols develop, decentralization enhances interoperability, making cross-network movement frictionless.
Reining in Big Tech remains an uphill battle, but in the meantime, the campaign offers a hilarious — and painfully accurate — look at the modern digital hellscape.
“The true mark of success for a project like this is when other people pick it up and run with it,” Doctorow said.
articles.summary:
The Norwegian Consumer Council has launched a satirical video campaign featuring the character Enshittificator to highlight how corporations deliberately degrade digital products and services to maximize short-term profits.

### Key Points
- The campaign, titled "Breaking Free," uses dark humor to critique planned obsolescence, subscription-based features, and the removal of essential product functionality.
- Author Cory Doctorow, who popularized the term "enshittification" in 2022, collaborated with the nonprofit to help expose corporate practices that prioritize revenue over consumer rights.
- The videos reference real-world examples, including Google Photos' storage caps, BMW’s subscription-based heated seats, and Apple’s "batterygate" settlement.
- The Norwegian Consumer Council advocates for policy reforms centered on interoperability, data portability, and the decentralization of social media to reduce Big Tech's market power.

HIFI Wants To Connect Bank Money, Stablecoins And Tokenized Assets
HIFI provides APIs designed to connect traditional bank rails with stablecoin settlement.
The company says its infrastructure currently processes more than $7 billion in annualized volume across 87 countries.
That business started largely around moving money.
The next stage is broader.
HIFI says the Series A will help expand card products, stablecoin payments and infrastructure used around tokenized securities and capital-market transactions.
The company participated in DTCC’s July production trades involving DTC-tokenized assets alongside firms including BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and Nasdaq.
It has also partnered with Visa on stablecoin-funded payouts that can reach billions of Visa cards.
Those integrations give HIFI a position between the blockchain layer and the financial institutions that ultimately need cash settlement, compliance and distribution.

Much of the attention around tokenization goes to the asset.
A Treasury security, stock or fund share gets represented onchain and suddenly the transaction looks modern.
But every trade still has another side.
Someone needs to deliver the money.
That is where stablecoin infrastructure becomes particularly interesting.
Tokenized capital markets work far better if the cash leg can move with the same speed and programmability as the security being traded.
HIFI is betting that the infrastructure connecting those two sides can become a substantial financial-services business.
The $37 million round does not come with a disclosed valuation.
It does provide the company with more capital to build into a market where traditional payments, stablecoins and securities settlement are increasingly converging.
Stablecoins used to be mostly a way for crypto traders to hold dollars between trades.

articles.title: Meta Made 43M Misleading Statements, New Mexico Jury Finds, Including on Its Cambridge Analytica Response
articles.author: EditorDavid
articles.content:
A New Mexico jury on Friday "found Facebook liable for deceiving users" about its privacy protections, reports the Associated Press.
 
A New Mexico newspaper calls it "another massive legal victory" against Facebook, reporting that the jury found Facebook "had committed tens of millions of violations of the state's Unfair Practices Act in connection with its lies to consumers about how their personal information was handled by the company and third-party users." The state has asked the company be ordered to pay the maximum civil penalty of $5,000 per violation meaning a judge could potentially order the company to pay billions in penalties to the state. The jury also found the company had been dishonest about its investigation of and response to the 2013 Cambridge Analytica data breach scandal, in which approximately 300,000 Facebook users took an online personality quiz, only to have the app that hosted the quiz harvest data from tens of millions of their "friends." The data was then transferred to the British consulting firm, which used it to create targeted political ads during the 2016 U.S. presidential election.
More details from Reuters: The verdict followed a two-week trial over a lawsuit filed by New Mexico's attorney general in 2021, three years after news reports revealed that the firm, Cambridge Analytica, had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app... At a press conference after the verdict was announced, New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said the case revealed "in stark detail the way in which this company plays fast and loose with the rules."
 
Jurors found 26 of 29 statements identified by the state were misleading, including comments about user data... Judge Francis Mathew will now determine civil penalties after jurors found more than 43 million violations, based on the number of people affected by the company's misleading statements... [New Mexico Attorney General] Torrez said his office is evaluating how much to seek but will push for the maximum penalty based on the jury's findings. The state will also ask [Judge] Mathew to direct Meta to make changes, which could include corrections to its past misstatements as well as an audit of the way it manages user data, Torrez said.

- Eligible Kraken users and customers of xStocks Alliance partners in more than 110 countries can register interest before the Nasdaq listing.

The Pre-IPO Step Is An Indication Of Interest
Eligible users can register a non-binding indication of interest ahead of Ōura’s planned Nasdaq listing.
That wording is important.
Registering does not guarantee an allocation, and users are not buying Ōura shares simply by submitting interest through Kraken or another xStocks Alliance platform.
If the IPO proceeds, Payward says Ōura will become the fourth company to move through its IPO Access pipeline this year.
The previous offerings covered SpaceX, Bending Spoons and Jersey Mike’s.
Eligible users in more than 110 countries can participate through Kraken and other supported xStocks partners.
The Tokenized Product Comes After The Listing
Payward says Ōura will be tokenized as ŌURAx on listing day.
That would turn the newly public stock into an xStocks product designed for round-the-clock blockchain-based trading.
The model extends what crypto exchanges have been doing with existing public stocks into the IPO process itself.
Instead of waiting for shares to begin trading and then creating tokenized exposure later, Payward is trying to connect the pre-IPO allocation process directly with the tokenized secondary market.
There are still several layers of eligibility and regulation involved.
An xStock is not the same thing as directly holding a conventional brokerage share, and tokenized equities are unavailable in a number of jurisdictions.
The pre-IPO indication is also explicitly non-binding.
Still, the product shows how quickly the line between crypto exchanges and conventional brokerage infrastructure is disappearing.
Kraken increasingly wants users to access crypto, tokenized stocks and now IPO-linked products through the same broader ecosystem.
If Ōura completes its listing as planned, the transition from private-company exposure to a tokenized public-market instrument could happen almost immediately.

articles.title: The Aosu R1 Ultra is a great subscription-free video, albeit with some minor flaws
articles.author: James Day
articles.content:
TechRadar Verdict
Buying a video doorbell usually comes with a rental agreement to store useful footage in the cloud, but the Aosu R1 Ultra sales pitch is slightly different. Clips land on the included AosuBase Mini with an 8GB capacity and 60 days of loop recording where nothing vital is paywalled. Daylight video is sharp, and AI detection holds up, but there are some caveats. Night vision is infrared only, recharging means unclipping the entire doorbell, and the spec sheet slightly oversells things. For example, 5MP UHD resolution isn’t true UHD, and 166-degree field of view isn’t what you’ll actually see, but if you buy it for what it does, rather than what it claims, this is a capable smart security investment.
Pros
- +Local storage with no subscription
- +Included base station with 8GB storage and 60-day loop
- +Decent radar and AI detection
- +Voice-disguise option for answering the door
- +Anti-tamper alert with local footage
- +Battery or wired installation
Cons
- -Infrared-only night vision
- -Whole unit removed to charge
- -Quick replies can't be edited or customised
- -Base station plugs in indefinitely
- -No Matter or HomeKit support
Why you can trust TechRadar
Aosu Video Doorbell R1 Ultra: two-minute review
Doorbell brands usually sell you the hardware cheap and charge you monthly for the privilege of seeing the footage. Aosu has gone the other way, and for that alone the R1 Ultra is worth your attention.
Video clips go to the AosuBase Mini, a small plug-in box that lives inside your house and does three jobs at once — Wi-Fi bridge, indoor chime, and storage. It holds 8GB and keeps a rolling 60 days of footage.
There is an optional cloud subscription, AosuProtect+, but unlike Ring's arrangement, the doorbell isn't hobbled without it. You get alerts, live view, two-way talk, custom detection zones, and full playback for nothing other than the purchase price.
Detection is another strength. Rather than relying on a passive infrared sensor and hoping, Aosu layers radar and AI human recognition on top, which lets it judge distance and intent — approaching versus passing, lingering versus walking through.
There's also a Tone button hiding in the two-way talk screen. Tap it, and you can answer the door as either 'uncle' or 'clown', with Aosu's straight-faced explanation that this disguises your voice for privacy.
The uncle setting artificially deepens voices, transitioning women and children to something resembling a man to deter would-be intruders. Clown goes all high-pitched and distorted to mask your identity.
Fortunately, the latter falls on the right side of sinister, so you can forget scaring off trick-or-treaters with imitations of South Park’s Mickey Mouse.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Where Aosu gets ahead of itself is resolution and framing. The sensor is 2560 x 1920, which is 4.9 megapixels in a 4:3 frame. That’s sharp, and a step up from 2K doorbells at this price, but not the claimed ‘UHD’, which would be 3,840 x 2,160.
The asserted 60% improvement over standard 2K only holds if the 2K you're comparing against is Aosu's own 3MP doorbell. An earlier version of the identical claim, on the identical camera, said 40%.
Field of view should be taken with a pinch of salt, too. Aosu says 166 degrees, but that's the corner-to-corner measurement. In reality, it's 133 horizontal by 103 vertical, shot in a shallow 4:3 aspect ratio and no head-to-toe image tricks.
With realistic use, the battery should last six months between charges. The kicker is the cell isn’t quick-release, and juicing it from flat to full takes six hours. So that means unclipping the entire doorbell and going without it for quite a while.
Aosu Video Doorbell R1 Ultra: price & availability
- List price: £139.99 / $135.99 (about AU$190)
- Launched July 2026 in the UK
- Available in the UK, US, and across the EU
With a list price of $135.99 / £139.99 (about AU$190), but usually discounted, the R1 Ultra is filed under ‘affordable’ and veers towards bargain territory if you find one hovering around the £100 mark. 
At that price, the value case is strong, because the base station is in the box rather than a £50 upsell, and the 60 days of local recording would cost you a subscription almost anywhere else.
Over three years, that's the difference between a hundred pounds and several hundred more.
- Value score: 4/5
Aosu Video Doorbell R1 Ultra: subscription costs
The R1 Ultra is fully functional without a subscription. Alerts, live view, two-way talk, detection zones, and 60 days of local playback are all included.
AosuProtect+ is the optional cloud add-on. In the UK, it's advertised at £9.99 (about $10 / AU$20) a month or £122.99 (about $160 / AU$230) a year, currently discounted to £3.49 (about $5 / AU$10) and £39.99 (about $50 / AU$80). Treat the higher figures with the same suspicion as the hardware list price.
The annual price is simply the monthly rate multiplied by twelve, so there's no built-in saving for paying up front, and £3.49 lands within pennies of what Aosu charges in dollars in the US. There’s a 30-day free trial if you wish to dip your toe.
What it buys you is cloud backup rather than capability: 14 or 30 days of event recordings, playback from anywhere, faster scrubbing, and bulk downloads. AI facial recognition sits on the top tier and is offered for video doorbells only.
The argument for paying is that local storage is bound to the base station like Bilbo Baggins is bound to the ring in The Lord of The Rings. If it fails, someone takes it, or you inexplicably drop it in the fires of Mount Doom, your footage dies with it.
Aosu Video Doorbell R1 Ultra: specs
| Feature | Specification | 
| Type | Battery-powered or hardwired video doorbell; base station required | 
| Resolution | 5MP (2560 x 1920) with WDR | 
| Zoom | 6 x digital | 
| View | 4:3 aspect ratio | 
| Field of view | 166 degrees diagonal [133 x 103 degrees] | 
| Night vision | Infrared up to 6 feet / 10m | 
| Audio | Two-way talk with voice disguise features | 
| Motion detection | Radar, PIR and AI human recognition; customizable zones | 
| Power | Rechargeable battery 5,000mAh, non-removable; USB-C cable included; 6 hours from flat; hardwire (8–24VAC) | 
| Connectivity | Doorbell 2.4GHz only; AosuBase Mini dual-band 2.4GHz / 5GHz | 
| Smart detection | AI human recognition; facial recognition requires AosuProtect+ | 
| Storage | Local, 8GB on AosuBase Mini, 60-day loop, no subscription; optional cloud with AosuProtect+ | 
| Smart home | Amazon Alexa, Google Assistant | 
| Tamper protection | Pry detection with chime alert; footage retained locally | 
| Weather | IP65 | 
| Finish | Black/silver | 
| Dimensions | 5 x 2 x 3 inches / 12.7 x 5.1 x 7.6cm | 
Aosu Video Doorbell R1 Ultra: design and installation
- Plain but solid
- Hub required indoors
- Battery or existing wiring
The R1 Ultra is a black plastic slab with silver flourishes similar to a Ring, and very little design ambition beyond flattering imitation.
Installation is straightforward and takes about half an hour all in. Bracket on the wall, doorbell clipped on top, base station plugged in somewhere central.
Aosu recommends mounting at 4 feet / 1.2 meters rather than eye-level, which is lower than instinct suggests but necessary if you want the frame to reach the doorstep. Worth getting right the first time rather than re-drilling.
A 15-degree wedge is included if you need to angle it towards a path or a gate, along with a screwdriver, extension wires and wire nuts for anyone hardwiring to existing 8–24V doorbell wiring.
The base station isn't optional, and it isn't outdoors-rated. It's the storage, the chime, and the Wi-Fi bridge in one. It needs a mains socket permanently, and it's rated only to 14°F / −10°C, so it lives in the hall or the cupboard under the stairs and stays there.
Detaching the whole unit from the wall for a full six-hour recharge via USB-C is a weak point, but a cable is bundled in the box.
A neat addition is pry detection. Try to lever the unit off its bracket, and it sounds a chime and pushes an alert, with footage on the base station indoors rather than on what’s being stolen.
- Design score: 3.5/5
Aosu Video Doorbell R1 Ultra: performance
- Sharp in daylight
- Strong multi-sensor detection
- Infrared-only after dark
Daylight is this doorbell’s happy place, with 5MP more than most similarly-priced rivals offer. Faces, delivery uniforms and parcel labels are legible rather than merely present.
Radar handles distance and movement, PIR picks up body heat, and the AI layer decides whether what it's looking at is a person. During testing, alerts felt instantaneous once someone reached the door.
After dark, expectations need managing. There is no color night vision and no spotlight.
Eight 850nm infrared LEDs offer monochrome up to 33 feet / 10 meters, and the manual warns mounting too close to a side wall will bounce IR back into the lens and fog the image. I’d pair the R1 Ultra with an outdoor light to make up for the shortfall.
Answering the door is well handled. Notifications arrive with a thumbnail of whatever triggered them, so you can tell a courier from a cat without opening the app, and tapping through starts a proper two-way video call rather than a one-way stream.
The 6x digital zoom lets you crop into a face or a label, though at 15fps and with a wide lens, it softens quickly.
Quick Reply issues an audible preset message when you can't talk. Somewhat boringly, they’re fixed, so you can’t edit the wording or add your own.
On connectivity, the doorbell itself is 2.4GHz only; the dual-band capability belongs to the AosuBase Mini, which talks to your router on 2.4 or 5GHz.
That's a sensible design for a battery device, but it means the camera-to-base link is on the crowded band and placement of the base matters more than usual. Plugged in 33 feet / 10 meters from my front door with the broadband router halfway, all was fine.
Live view includes a UHD/SD toggle to drop the quality when the connection struggles, and you can save a clip or a still straight to your phone's camera roll if you ever need to hand something to a neighbor or the police.
The six-month battery figure assumes up to ten events a day at 20 seconds each — about three-and-a-half minutes of recording daily. On a busy porch with a path or pavement in frame, expect considerably less.
- Performance score: 3/5
Should you buy the Aosu Video Doorbell R1 Ultra?
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | Local storage, included base station, and no monthly fee at around £100 make the maths hard to argue with. | 4/5 | 
| Design | Solid and easy to install, but the base station needs a permanent socket, and recharging equals doorbell removal. | 3.5/5 | 
| Performance | Sharp daylight video and excellent multi-sensor detection, let down by infrared-only night vision and overstated specs. | 3/5 | 
Buy it if
You're sick of subscriptions
Sixty days of local recording on the included base, with nothing important behind a paywall, is undoubtedly attractive.
You'd rather not be yourself
Uncle and clown voice settings let anyone home alone answer the door sounding like someone else.
You want fewer useless alerts
The radar, PIR, and AI combination is a real step up from the single-sensor budget crowd, and it shows in your notification tray.
You have existing doorbell wiring
Hardwiring to 8–24V takes the recharging problem off the table entirely, and this is one of the cheaper doorbells that supports it.
Don't buy it if
You need to see faces after dark
Infrared monochrome to 33 feet / 10 meters is all you get. There's no spotlight and no color low-light mode, so a night clip tells you someone was there, but not necessarily who.
You don’t want to remove the doorbell
No quick-release battery means every recharge is a six-hour outage with the unit off the wall and on your kitchen counter.
Aosu Video Doorbell R1 Ultra: also consider
Ring Battery Video Doorbell (2nd Gen)
Cheaper, shoots Retinal 2K with a genuine head-to-toe 1:1 view and color night vision, and installs without a hub. The trade-off is Ring's subscription model and Amazon's data record.
Eufy Video Doorbell C31
The closest like-for-like on the no-monthly-fee promise, with 2K video and a quick-release battery, though you'll want a HomeBase to get the most from it.
How I tested the Aosu Video Doorbell R1 Ultra
- Fitted to a domestic front door
- Assessed daylight and infrared video, detection accuracy, and audio
- Ran entirely without a subscription
I mounted the R1 Ultra on my own front door and used it as the household's main entry camera for a fortnight, deliberately running it on local storage alone so the no-subscription claim could be tested as most buyers will experience it.
I checked live-view responsiveness and alert latency, reviewed clips in daylight and after dark, and tracked battery drain against Aosu's 180-day claim.

- The device features a 5MP sensor with radar and AI human recognition to minimize false alerts and improve detection accuracy.
- Installation supports both battery-powered and hardwired configurations, though the battery requires removing the entire unit for a six-hour recharge.
- Night vision is limited to infrared monochrome, lacking the color low-light modes or integrated spotlights found on some competitors.
- The doorbell includes unique privacy features like voice-disguise options and anti-tamper alerts that trigger a chime if the unit is removed.

### Why it Matters
This device challenges the industry-standard model of locking essential security features behind recurring monthly subscription fees. By prioritizing local storage and robust hardware, it provides a cost-effective alternative for homeowners seeking privacy and long-term value without ongoing service costs.

articles.title: watchOS 27: 12 New Things To Check Out on Your Apple Watch
articles.author: Tim Hardwick
articles.content:
Apple released watchOS 27 on September 14. The features and changes aren't limited to owners of new Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 models. If you have an Apple Watch model that supports the latest update, here are 12 features and changes to check out after installation.
To do so, open the Watch app on your iPhone, then tap General ➝ Software Update, strap your watch into a charger, and follow the onscreen prompts.
Check Out the Dedicated Siri App
Siri has finally caught up with the AI revolution, and apart from having contextual awareness, it now has an app of its own that collects every conversation in a single view and syncs them privately across your devices over iCloud. Just ask something on your iPhone and you can pick the thread up again on your Apple Watch, as well as pin conversations worth keeping, or even start a new chat directly from your wrist.
Try Siri Modular Watch Face
The new Siri watch face is a genuinely useful one. Its rectangular complication shows you whatever sits at the top of your Smart Stack, and it automatically updates through the day based on time, location, and other factors.
The Dynamic App Grid
Pressing the Digital Crown no longer produces the honeycomb app view by default. Now, watchOS 27 shows a dynamic grid made up of suggested apps, your most-used apps, and your most recently used ones. The Siri app sits in the middle, but the alphabetical list remains available – simply turn the Digital Crown to navigate through all of your apps.
New Tap Gesture
Apple has added a third gesture to Double Tap and Wrist Flick. The new one is simply called Tap. A single tap of your index finger and thumb opens the highlighted widget in the Smart Stack. You can still navigate the Smart Stack with Double Tap and dismiss notifications with Wrist Flick.
Walkie-Talkie Has Been Deleted
Walkie-Talkie is gone, and not merely hidden. The app is unavailable after updating to watchOS 27 and cannot be reinstalled from the App Store. You can keep the app by staying on watchOS 26, but you won't be able to start a conversation with a contact who has updated.
Live Rewind (Not Yet)
This is the change most likely to catch people out. In watchOS 26 and earlier, a double press of the Digital Crown opens the App Switcher, where you can jump back to the previous app, scroll through recent ones, and swipe to force-quit anything misbehaving.
That's changed in watchOS 27, in which a double press shows the new dynamic app grid instead. The gesture has been reserved for Live Rewind, an upcoming feature (exclusive to Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4) that produces a transcript of the last fifteen seconds of speech in your environment.
Fortunately, the App Switcher will still be available when watchOS 27.2 is released later this year, but it will open with a different gesture. If you're already on the latest beta, simply long press on the bottom of the app that you're in, and that should open the App Switcher.
Find My is Now One App
Find Devices, Find Items, and Find People have been folded into a single Find My app with a map-centric layout, which also includes shortcuts for directions and for items nearby. 
Workout Buddy No Longer Needs Your iPhone
Introduced in watchOS 26, Workout Buddy previously required your iPhone within range. In watchOS 27, your Apple Watch can run it if Wi-Fi or cellular is available. It also draws new insights from your training history, tracking gradual gains in pace, distance and workout duration, and it now speaks Spanish as well as English.
New Cycle Tracking Features
Cycle Tracking in the Health app can now notify you if your logged patterns are suggestive of perimenopause, alongside symptom tracking and educational material. The notifications only draw on your logged cycle history and apply to users aged 40 and over. Apple says the feature is not a method of birth control and is not a diagnosis.
Treadmill Distance Is More Accurate
In watchOS 27, new machine learning motion algorithms measure distance more precisely for indoor runs and walks, and Apple says the improvement starts from the first step, as opposed to settling after a few minutes. Fitness route maps are more accurate too, and step counts finally stay in sync between the Fitness and Health apps.
The Smart Stack Gets More to Say
The Smart Stack's contextual suggestions are now a lot smarter. A few examples provided by Apple include new widgets surfacing your parked car's location, a close contact's birthday, a change in your transit card balance, the Noise app immediately after a loud-noise alert, a reminder that Theater Mode is still on, pinned messages, celebrations, and identity cards.
New Models Get a Steps Counter
On Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, the redesigned pedometer model and S11 chip allow watchOS 27 to provide more accurate step counts. There's also a new Steps complication on the latest models to track your steps in real time, right from your watch face. Will we see the feature come to older devices? Your guess is as good as ours.
articles.summary:
Apple released watchOS 27 on September 14, introducing a dedicated Siri app, a redesigned dynamic app grid, enhanced fitness tracking capabilities, and significant changes to navigation gestures.

### Key Points
- The new Siri app enables cross-device conversation syncing via iCloud and features a contextual Siri Modular watch face.
- A new "Tap" gesture allows users to open Smart Stack widgets, while the Walkie-Talkie app has been permanently removed.
- The Find My app now consolidates device, item, and people tracking into a single, map-centric interface.
- Workout Buddy no longer requires an iPhone connection, and indoor treadmill distance tracking now utilizes improved machine learning algorithms.
- Cycle Tracking now includes notifications for patterns suggestive of perimenopause for users aged 40 and older.
- Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 models receive exclusive features, including a real-time steps complication and the upcoming Live Rewind transcription tool.

### Why it Matters
These updates represent a significant shift in how users interact with their Apple Watch by prioritizing AI-driven contextual information and streamlining navigation. The removal of legacy features alongside new health and fitness capabilities signals Apple's ongoing effort to position the device as a standalone health-monitoring tool.

articles.title: Google Photos causes headaches: users say editing pictures makes the app 'unresponsive'
articles.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
articles.content:
What you need to know
- Pixel users say Google Photos is causing problems when editing images as it becomes "unresponsive."
- Many Pixel users on Reddit report similarities, as the app's UI options become useless despite the lack of an error message.
- Google responded to the thread; however, the suggested actions have not worked, and users have been encouraged to submit a proper bug report.
Pixel users are encountering a few frustrating issues late this week in Google Photos. They claim that certain actions make the entire app unresponsive.
Reports were spotted today (Sept. 25) on Reddit (via Android Authority). One report by a user with a Pixel 11 Pro XL says the app becomes unresponsive after editing a photo. In this particular instance, the user was cropping a photo of a newspaper. However, when they finished, they said, "the resulting photo becomes completely unresponsive to several actions." The user provided a video with their Reddit report.
It showed them trying to tap every button on the bottom nav bar: Share, Edit, and Trash. Nothing works. Tapping "Add To" brings up the folder menu, but that's hardly useful in this situation. One user said, "I did exactly what you did. Took a picture, edit, crop, save. Opened the photo gallery, none of the options are responsive."
Here's where things evolve. Google responded to the user's report, offering aid; however, nothing seems to have worked. The user states they've attempted their suggestions, as well as suggestions by Google support—nothing has worked. The user was then advised to file an official bug report, meaning this issue might require more attention.
Problems right after an update
What's unclear is whether this problem is the result of the latest Google Photos update. We covered the huge app update yesterday, which brings Gemini Spark integration into the mix for Android users. Users can write a prompt to the AI, telling it the changes they'd like to be made. If people are lingering in the background, you can remove them and brighten those that matter. Another huge part of this update was "Moods."
Moods are new styles ("more than filters," per Google) that can give your photos a different feel. If you're going for a vintage aesthetic, there are Moods to choose from. What's more, Google introduced a new "redact pen" to help users blur sensitive details in images.
